reviewer: Codex /root/kings_19_22 (AI-assisted supplied-English author curation for 2 Kings 22–25)
review_method: Read all 107 complete actual source units in 2 Kings 22–25, every proposed retained target, and necessary surrounding context through complete_text before generating the first retained draft. Read complete 2 Chronicles 34–36 including lettered continuations, actual Jeremiah 52 with its supplied gaps, law contexts in Deuteronomy and Exodus 12, Bethel oracle and burial context in 1 Kings 13, earlier temple-repair context in 2 Kings 12, and Manasseh context in 2 Kings 21. Separately reread every one of the 112 complete source/target/category/rationale triples in five bounded displays of 22,23,22,23,22 with no clipping. Preserved the original draft and a coherent nine-triple author precision stage. All nine corrected full triples were separately displayed and reread before freeze. Same-chapter categories were explicitly marked from the first draft and pass the exact iff gate. The five additional pairs concern a second faithful-worker statement, the exact torn-garment response, law language about whole heart and soul, tomb identification before exemption, and the threefold heart/soul/strength command; they are particular supported connections, not generic padding. This initial curated supplied-English pass is not exhaustive cross-reference discovery, original-language or apparatus certification, independent human specialist approval, or a solution to numerical, genealogical, geographical, or regnal differences.
pin_method: Fresh raw GitHub fetch of every one of six retained source/target books at the fixed commit; exact Git blob rehash against saved source registries and full parsed JSON cache equality, with saved raw bytes and SHA256 receipts. Recorded newline differences do not change parsed content. Inventory, parsing, and pin verification add zero completed reading credit.

before.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: tomb identification and exemption
before.rationale: After the men identify the marker as the man of God's tomb, Josiah commands that its bones be left alone. The identification supplies the particular narrated reason for treating that tomb differently from the bones burned on the altar.

after.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: tomb identification and exemption
after.rationale: After the men identify the marker as the man of God's tomb, Josiah commands that its bones be left alone. The identification immediately precedes the different treatment of that tomb from the bones burned on the altar; no additional unspoken motive is assigned.

changes.reason: Retain the narrated sequence without labeling an unstated motive as an explicit reason.

before.rationale: Both assess Josiah's Passover as unmatched in the earlier royal period. Kings extends its comparison to the days of the judges, whereas Chronicles says since Samuel the prophet; these different comparison expressions remain as supplied, without a period equation.

after.rationale: Kings says this Passover had not occurred since the days of the judges, throughout Israel and Judah's royal days; Chronicles says no Passover like it had occurred since Samuel the prophet. The distinct comparison expressions are retained without making them an identical period or an absolute assertion that no Passover had ever been observed in between.

changes.reason: Retain this Passover versus no Passover like it, and judges versus Samuel, without broadening the comparison.

before.rationale: Both declare no comparable king before or after Josiah, describing his return to the Lord with whole heart, soul, and strength according to Moses' law. This compares the explicit evaluation without claiming the entire deeds of every other king have been independently examined.

after.rationale: Both give the no-one-like-him assessment in Josiah's royal context, describing his return to the Lord with whole heart, soul, and strength according to Moses' law. Kings explicitly says no king like him, while Chronicles says no one like him; those scopes remain as supplied without claiming an independent review of every earlier person's deeds.

changes.reason: Retain the source no-king scope and target no-one scope.

before.relationship: Parallel Egyptian confrontation with unresolved death sequence
before.rationale: Both describe Egypt's ruler going against Assyria at the Euphrates and Josiah going to meet him. Kings says Nechao killed Josiah at Mageddo when he saw him; Chronicles narrates archers wounding him, transport to Jerusalem, and death. The bounded campaign connection does not reconcile those differing death sequences or name forms.

after.relationship: Parallel Egyptian confrontation with unresolved death sequence
after.rationale: Both describe Egypt's ruler going against Assyria at the Euphrates and Josiah going to meet him. Kings says Nechao killed Josiah at Mageddo when he saw him; Chronicles narrates archers shooting at him, his report of great pain, transport to Jerusalem, and death. The bounded campaign connection does not reconcile those differing death sequences or name forms.

changes.reason: Retain the explicit archers-shot-at clause and report of pain rather than an imported wounding verb.

before.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: besieging king and Judean surrender
before.rationale: Babylon's king enters while his servants besiege Jerusalem; Joakim and the listed royal company then go out to him and are taken. The target gives the particular surrender and capture, without deriving whose eighth regnal year is meant from outside the actual wording.

after.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: besieging king and Judean surrender
after.rationale: Babylon's king enters while his servants besiege Jerusalem; Joakim and the listed royal company then go out to him, and Babylon's king takes him. The target gives this particular royal surrender and capture without extending the singular him to a separately stated capture of every companion or independently deriving whose eighth regnal year is meant.

changes.reason: Retain the singular him in the capture clause; no separately stated capture of every companion.

before.relationship: Temple and royal treasures carried to Babylon in separate deportation notices
before.rationale: Kings narrates removal of temple and royal treasures and cutting apart Solomon's gold vessels; Chronicles likewise names temple vessels and royal treasures brought to Babylon. The particular plunder motif is compared without making the different siege episodes identical or inserting the gold-cutting action into Chronicles.

after.relationship: Temple and royal treasures in separate deportation notices
after.rationale: Kings narrates removal of temple and royal treasures and cutting apart Solomon's gold vessels; Chronicles likewise names temple vessels and royal treasures brought to Babylon. The particular plunder motif is compared without making the different siege episodes identical or inserting the gold-cutting action into Chronicles.

changes.reason: The source verse reports removal without separately stating the destination; the target supplies its own Babylon destination.

before.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: repeated father-pattern evil assessment
before.rationale: Sedekias does evil according to Joakim's deeds; the earlier new king's assessment likewise says evil according to his father's deeds. The repeated assessment is compared without using the repeated Joakim name to manufacture an additional family relationship for Sedekias.

after.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: repeated evil assessment
after.rationale: Sedekias does evil according to Joakim's deeds; the earlier new king's assessment likewise says evil according to his father's deeds. The repeated assessment is compared without using the repeated Joakim name to manufacture an additional family relationship for Sedekias.

changes.reason: Remove a father-pattern category that could imply an unestablished Sedekias parentage.

before.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: assassination followed by flight to Egypt
before.rationale: The people and force commanders leave for Egypt from fear of the Chaldeans after Ishmael kills Godolias and those with him. The action follows that specific violence; the source does not independently narrate a Chaldean retaliatory attack before their departure.

after.relationship: Same-chapter literary parallel: assassination followed by flight to Egypt
after.rationale: The people and force commanders leave for Egypt from fear of the Chaldeans after Ishmael strikes Godolias, who dies, and the Judeans and Chaldeans with him. The action follows that specific violence; the source does not separately state that every other person struck died or narrate a Chaldean retaliatory attack before the departure.

changes.reason: Only Godolias is explicitly said to die in the preceding actual unit; others are struck.

before.relationship: Partial royal release parallel with differing day unresolved
before.rationale: Both place the deported Judean king's prison release in the thirty-seventh deportation year and twelfth month, at the new Babylonian king's accession period. Kings gives the twenty-seventh day and Jeremiah the twenty-fourth. The release and shared year/month form the bounded connection; the day difference and name forms receive no independent reconciliation credit.

after.relationship: Partial royal release parallel with differing day unresolved
after.rationale: Both place the deported Judean king's prison release in the thirty-seventh deportation year and twelfth month. Kings gives the twenty-seventh day and says in the year of his reign; Jeremiah gives the twenty-fourth day and says in the year he became king. The release and shared year/month form the bounded connection; the day and regnal expressions remain distinct with no independent reconciliation credit.

changes.reason: The source does not independently identify the stated year of his reign as the accession year.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed reconciliation of Josiah death sequence and location; no death-sequence reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Kings states that Nechao killed Josiah at Mageddo when he saw him, and the following Kings unit transports him dead to Jerusalem. Chronicles narrates archers shooting at Josiah, his report of great pain, transport to Jerusalem, and then death. The retained partial connection is the explicit Egyptian Euphrates campaign and Josiah confrontation, while the differing death sequence remains unresolved.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed tribute-amount harmonization; no numerical reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Both passages supply one hundred talents of silver and Pharaoh removing the Judean king from Jerusalem rule; Kings gives one hundred talents of gold and Chronicles gives one talent of gold. The bounded removal-and-silver correspondence is retained without reconciling the gold amounts.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed prison-release date and regnal-expression harmonization; no date reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Both passages locate the royal prison release in the thirty-seventh deportation year and twelfth month. Kings gives the twenty-seventh day and in the year of his reign; Jeremiah gives the twenty-fourth day and in the year he became king. The release and shared year/month are retained without equating the day or regnal expressions or independently certifying the name forms.

candidate_exclusions.reason: These unestablished claims and all proposed identity/numerical/regnal/geographical harmonizations receive zero completion credit. Retained rationales preserve bounded literal correspondences and explicitly retain supplied differences.
